North Korea’s Kim urges wider tactical nuclear weapons deployment on facility tour, KCNA says

Reuters

26 November, 2026 06:30 am IST

By Kyu-seok Shim SEOUL, Nov 26 (Reuters) – North Korean leader Kim Jong Un said his country should focus on deploying tactical nuclear weapons across multiple domains and that its nuclear material production capacity was being systematically expanded, state media KCNA reported on Thursday.

Kim, who spoke during an inspection on Wednesday of nuclear material production and weapons research facilities, also said North Korea’s status as a nuclear weapons state was “absolutely inviolable”.

KCNA did not identify the facilities or their locations.

Show Full Article

“Our nuclear capability is now a reality,” KCNA quoted Kim as saying.

Kim said North Korea should “focus on utilising tactical nuclear weapons across multiple domains for different missions” and called recent achievements in nuclear weapons production a major success for the country’s nuclear force policy.

The tour of the nuclear facilities appears aimed at underscoring Pyongyang’s push to expand and diversify its nuclear arsenal in defiance of calls for denuclearisation, as questions persist over prospects for renewed dialogue with the United States.

Tactical nuclear weapons are generally lower-yield warheads meant for battlefield use, unlike strategic weapons designed for longer-range strikes.

In 2023, KCNA published images of what it called the Hwasan-31 tactical nuclear warhead, saying it could be fitted to a range of delivery systems, including short-range missiles.

Photographs released by KCNA on Thursday showed Kim and officials inspecting objects that analysts said looked like gas centrifuges, used to enrich uranium, and miniaturised, standardised tactical nuclear warheads such as the Hwasan-31.

Kim also said any attempt to deny North Korea’s nuclear status, which it enshrined in its constitution in 2023, would be regarded as “an open declaration of war”.

“Our possession of nuclear weapons is an absolutely irreversible choice as long as malicious forces exist that use nuclear weapons as a means of achieving hegemony,” Kim said.

KIM CITES US NUCLEAR ALLIANCES

Kim justified the buildup by citing what he described as growing nuclear threats from the United States and its allies.

The United States had “incited its vassal states” near North Korea to acquire nuclear-powered submarines by introducing the “dangerous precedent of nuclear proliferation through AUKUS to Northeast Asia,” he said, referring to the trilateral security pact involving the United States, Britain and Australia.

He also accused Washington of building a “nuclear military alliance system” by trying to share and use nuclear weapons with its allies.

South Korea is pursuing nuclear-powered submarines after US President Donald Trump approved the plan in October last year. The topic has also been under discussion in Japan.

Analysts said the visit carried a message for Washington amid speculation about US-North Korea diplomatic contact.

“This is not so much North Korea permanently closing the door to dialogue with the United States as a strategy of raising the bar: ‘denuclearisation talks’ are over, and if talks open in future, it will deal only on a ‘nuclear state versus nuclear state’ basis,” said Lim Eul-chul, a professor at South Korea’s Kyungnam University.

Shin Jong-woo, secretary-general of the Korea Defence and Security Forum, said Kim’s reference to “multiple domains” could signal targets beyond the Korean peninsula, including the US mainland.

Kim’s intent “seems to be that with no alternatives now, Pyongyang will build up its nuclear forces further and head toward a setup in which it can confront the US,” Shin said.

North Korea has conducted six nuclear tests since 2006, with its last and most powerful test in 2017.

South Korea’s defence minister said in August that Pyongyang was believed to possess between 80 and 120 nuclear warheads, but said the estimate came from private research organisations and could not be officially confirmed.

(Reporting by Kyu-seok Shim; Editing by Edmund Klamann and Ed Davies)

By Enas Alashray and Yomna Ehab CAIRO, Nov 25 (Reuters) – Thirty-one people were killed and 21 wounded in a fire after a vehicle carrying petroleum products overturned on a major ring road in Egypt, authorities said on Wednesday.

The fire broke out above a tunnel in Giza’s Al-Warraq district, the public prosecution said. Preliminary estimates found that 27 vehicles, including cars and motorcycles, had been charred, it said, adding that casualty figures and damage were still being assessed.

The prosecution ordered DNA samples to be taken from the bodies of victims who had not yet been identified to establish their identities.

Show Full Article

Thirty-nine ambulances took part in rescue operations, the health ministry said.

Videos circulating on social media showed thick plumes of smoke billowing from the scene.

Reuters verified the location from the buildings and road layout, which matched archive and satellite imagery of the area. The date was confirmed through the original file’s metadata. The date was also confirmed through local media reports and a statement from the health ministry.

“The cars were charred, with people inside them. They did not have time to get out,” Ali Youssef, who was at the scene, said. “The fire burned the vehicles and the people inside.”

Reuters footage from the scene in Giza showed firefighting vehicles, charred cars and minibuses, burnt motorcycles and debris scattered across the major ring road, while people and security personnel inspected the aftermath and a bulldozer moved damaged vehicles.

The ring road connects key highways across Greater Cairo, linking the governorates of Cairo, Giza and Qalyubia.

Road accidents are common in Egypt due to factors including speeding, weak enforcement of traffic regulations and poor road conditions.

The number of people killed in road accidents rose 10.8% to 5,829 in 2025 from 5,260 a year earlier, according to the state statistics agency CAPMAS.

Egypt has expanded its road network in recent years, building highways and bridges under a broader infrastructure programme aimed at easing congestion and accommodating rapid population growth and urban expansion. The projects have improved traffic flow in some areas, but concerns over road safety persist.

(Reporting by Yomna Ehab and Enas Alashray; Additional Reporting by Fernando Robles, María Paula Laguna and Sayed Sheashaa; Editing by Timothy Heritage, Mark Potter and Alistair Bell)

US proposes surprise new tariffs on Brazil imports, including 10% duty on aircraft

By Andrea Shalal and David Lawder WASHINGTON, Nov 25 (Reuters) – The United States proposed adding new tariffs on goods from Brazil on Wednesday, including a 10% duty on finished aircraft, saying Brasilia had failed to rectify what Washington calls “unreasonable” trade practices.

The move is part of a broader round of tariffs the Trump administration has announced on goods from more than a dozen trading partners. It caught Brazil off guard just a month after a presidential election in which US tariffs and influence featured heavily.

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said his office was proposing changes to tariffs imposed in July after Brazil made “no meaningful progress” on the issues. The changes would give Washington more leverage to pressure Brazil to drop the practices, he said.

Show Full Article

Brazil was the first country targeted under US President Donald Trump’s new tariff strategy, which relies on Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, an unfair trade practices statute. The US Supreme Court struck down Trump’s previous global tariffs under an emergency law, including duties of up to 50% on Brazilian goods, in February.

Under the proposal, finished Brazilian aircraft, which are currently exempt, would face a 10% duty. Aircraft are Brazil’s fourth-largest export to the United States, and the measure could hit planemaker Embraer hard.

The company’s shares were down over 3% on Wednesday afternoon. The company said in a statement it was reviewing the US government’s announcement, adding that Embraer “continues to believe in and strongly defends maintaining the zero-tariff regime for the global aerospace industry, which has been in place since the 1980s.”

Two people at the company, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said the announcement was a surprise.

Aerospace has largely escaped the tariffs that have hit other sectors such as autos, steel and aluminum. But tariffs on Embraer commercial jets would pose problems for US airlines, which have no domestic alternative for flying regional routes to smaller cities.

NEW SUGAR DUTY PROPOSED

Washington is also proposing a new tariff rate on out-of-quota raw and refined sugar that enters the US on a nondiscriminatory basis, the US Trade Representative’s office said. This would ensure that sugar from Brazil could not be shipped through third countries into the United States.

The impact may be limited, however. Brazil’s sugar exports to the US have dwindled to just over 146,000 tons in 2026 through the end of October, down from more than 1 million metric tons in 2024, according to industry body UNICA.

The US already plans to cut Brazil’s tariff-free raw sugar quota for 2027 by about a third, to 100,000 tons.

Renato Cunha, CEO of industry group NovaBio, said the new tariff will not directly affect producers in Brazil’s north and northeast, which benefit from the quota, though he called the tariff “negative” and said it “highlights the unpredictability of these actions interfering in the market.”

Greer said the sugar and aircraft duties were meant to bring Brazil to the negotiating table, and that Washington remains open to talks.

Washington accuses Brazil of unfair practices on a range of issues from illegal deforestation to Brazil’s instant payment system, Pix, which the US government argues disadvantages credit card companies. Brasilia has rejected all the allegations.

Brazil’s Foreign Ministry said the government would assess the impacts and repercussions of the proposed tariffs.

Brazil and the US established a working group in September to drive negotiations over tariffs and a broader bilateral trade framework after a call between President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Trump, but Brazilian officials say a proposal from Washington that Brasilia had expected never materialized.

Lula won a new term in late October, defeating right-wing opponent Flavio Bolsonaro, who had campaigned on stronger ties with the Trump administration. During the campaign, Lula described US tariffs on Brazilian goods as election interference meant to benefit his opponent.

Brazil asked on Tuesday for the creation of a dispute panel at the World Trade Organization to examine the July Section 301 tariffs, a move the US blocked the same day.

A person in Lula’s government, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said the announcement surprised the government, which thought Brazil would not be included in a new round of US tariffs.

The July tariffs, which followed months of fruitless negotiations between US and Brazilian officials, had maintained and expanded exemptions for Brazilian beef, coffee, aircraft and other goods.

Brazil also faces an additional 12.5% tariff under a separate Section 301 investigation into connections to forced labor in the supply chains of dozens of countries.

The USTR will hold a hearing on the duties on January 14, before they can take effect.

(Reporting by Andrea Shalal and David Lawder; additional reporting by Jasper Ward and Gabriel Araujo; Writing by David Lawder and Brendan O’Boyle; editing by Lincoln Feast, Rod Nickel and Sanjeev Miglani)
